name: Physical Education
description: Foundational concepts in physical fitness, exercise science, and lifelong wellness habits. Students explore the five components of fitness, movement skills, sport participation, and healthy lifestyle design.

modules.title: Introduction to Physical Fitness
modules.objectives: Define physical fitness; identify its five health-related components; understand why each matters for lifelong health. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: CDC — Physical Activity Basics — for background reading on Introduction to Physical Fitness before the quiz and assignment
modules.videoNote: GIIS Physical Education — Module 1: Introduction to Physical Fitness — reviewed lesson video for this module.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Compare these supplied fictional profiles using the five health-related fitness components: Avery can walk briskly for 30 minutes and complete 18 controlled squats but cannot yet hold a plank for 20 seconds; Rowan can hold a 45-second plank and complete 12 controlled push-ups but needs a rest after 8 minutes of brisk walking. Neither profile includes body-composition measurements. For each profile, identify one strength, one area to develop, and one safe one-week plan. Submit: a one-page comparison table plus a 100-word rationale. Include: the required artifact, specific evidence from the fictional or provided data, and a brief explanation of the major choices. Evaluation: all five components are used accurately; recommendations match the evidence; FITT choices are specific; and the rationale explains one revision after self-check. Do not use or disclose your own health or fitness data.

modules.title: The FITT Principle
modules.objectives: Explain Frequency, Intensity, Time, and Type; use the FITT principle to design and justify a safe paper plan for a provided fictional beginner. Students will connect each variable to the fictional profile, use conditional progression and recovery rules, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment; no personal health or fitness disclosure is required.
modules.readingNote: CDC — Physical Activity Guidelines for School-Aged Children and Adolescents — age-appropriate background, not a prescription for one workout. FITT planning guide: Frequency is how often; Intensity is how hard; Time is minutes or repetitions; Type is the activity. Talk-test moderate effort means a learner can talk but not sing. For the fictional plan, walking develops cardiovascular endurance and controlled wall push-ups or resistance-band movements develop muscular endurance. Place demanding muscular-endurance sessions on nonconsecutive days. Progress one variable only after the current workload remains comfortable with controlled form; hold or reduce for unusual fatigue or loss of form, and stop a painful activity and tell a responsible adult or qualified professional.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Physical Education — Module 2: The FITT Principle — reviewed lesson video for this module.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the Module 2 FITT planning guide and fictional Jordan profile. Start from Jordan’s stated baseline. Two acceptable conditional progression examples are adding five minutes to one walking session or adding one controlled muscular-endurance set only after the prior workload remains comfortable; a valid plan may hold or reduce workload instead. No external account or personal health data is required.
modules.assignment: Provided fictional profile: Jordan is 14, currently walks comfortably for 20 minutes twice weekly at a talk-test effort and completes two controlled sets of eight wall push-ups on two nonconsecutive days. Jordan has three available activity days, access to a safe walking route and a resistance band, and reports no current pain. This is a paper-planning task, not personal exercise advice. Design a four-week FITT plan for Jordan that develops cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance. Include frequency, intensity, time, and type for each week and explain two gradual, conditional progressions tied to the profile. Examples include adding five minutes to one walking session or adding one controlled muscular-endurance set only after the prior workload remains comfortable with controlled form. Keep demanding muscular-endurance sessions nonconsecutive. Hold or reduce workload for unusual fatigue or loss of form; stop a painful activity and tell a responsible adult or qualified professional. Submit: a calendar and a 150-word justification. Include: specific evidence from the fictional profile, reasons for the major choices, and one hold-or-reduce rule. Evaluation: all FITT variables are present; progression is conditional and gradual; activities match the two target components; and safety limits are clear. Do not use or disclose personal health or fitness data.

modules.title: Cardiovascular Endurance
modules.objectives: Define cardiovascular endurance; explain heart and lung responses to aerobic exercise; identify activities that build aerobic fitness. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: CDC — Physical Activity for Adults — for background reading on Cardiovascular Endurance before the quiz and assignment
modules.videoNote: GIIS Physical Education — Module 3: Cardiovascular Endurance — reviewed lesson video for this module.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Analyze this supplied fictional table: Session 1 — resting heart rate 72 bpm, activity 12 minutes, perceived exertion 4/10; Session 2 — 70 bpm, 16 minutes, 5/10; Session 3 — 71 bpm, 20 minutes, 7/10. Graph one measure, describe the pattern, and recommend one evidence-based adjustment for the next session. Submit: the graph and a 150-word analysis. Include: the required artifact, specific evidence from the fictional or provided data, and a brief explanation of the major choices. Evaluation: the graph is accurate; the cardiovascular response is explained; the recommendation follows the data; and limitations are acknowledged. No personal exercise or heart-rate disclosure is required.

modules.title: Muscular Strength and Endurance
modules.objectives: Distinguish muscular strength from muscular endurance; identify major muscle groups; describe resistance training principles for each quality. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: NSCA — Education Articles index — use an article on resistance-training principles or muscle physiology for this module's background reading.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Physical Education — Module 4: Muscular Strength and Endurance — reviewed lesson video for this module.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Use these supplied fictional results to distinguish muscular strength from muscular endurance: Casey — 20 controlled wall push-ups, 55-second wall sit, 6 controlled repetitions with the heavier classroom resistance band; Morgan — 11 controlled wall push-ups, 35-second wall sit, 10 controlled repetitions with the same band. Then design a two-week resistance plan for one profile. Submit: a comparison table and plan. Include: the required artifact, specific evidence from the fictional or provided data, and a brief explanation of the major choices. Evaluation: strength and endurance are distinguished correctly; exercises match the target muscles; overload is gradual; and technique or supervision limits are stated.

modules.title: Flexibility and Stretching
modules.objectives: Define flexibility; distinguish static, dynamic, and PNF stretching; explain appropriate uses and limits of stretching in warm-ups, cool-downs, and flexibility training. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Physical Education — Module 5: Flexibility and Stretching — reviewed lesson video for this module.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Create a ten-minute warm-up and flexibility plan for a fictional recreational athlete. Label each activity as dynamic, static, or PNF; place it at an appropriate point in the session; and explain one benefit and one limitation of each method. Submit: a sequence chart and 150-word rationale. Include: the required artifact, specific evidence from the fictional or provided data, and a brief explanation of the major choices. Evaluation: classifications are accurate; timing is appropriate; claims avoid guarantees; and the plan includes a safe modification.

modules.title: Body Composition
modules.objectives: Define body composition and distinguish lean mass from fat mass; calculate BMI; explain why adolescent BMI uses age-and-sex percentiles and serves only as a screening measure; compare BMI with other information used to understand body composition.
modules.readingNote: CDC — Assessing Your Weight: BMI — for background reading on Body Composition before the quiz and assignment
modules.videoNote: GIIS Physical Education — Module 6: Body Composition — reviewed lesson video for this module.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Using this supplied fictional screening table, interpret rather than recalculate the results: Profile A — BMI-for-age percentile 62, CDC category healthy weight; Profile B — BMI-for-age percentile 91, CDC category overweight. Explain why BMI-for-age is a screening measure rather than a direct measure of body fat. Recommend one additional type of information a qualified health professional would consider. Submit: a completed interpretation table and a 200-word comparison. Include: the required artifact, specific evidence from the fictional or provided data, and a brief explanation of the major choices. Evaluation: percentile categories are interpreted accurately; limitations are explained; conclusions avoid diagnosis; and no personal measurements are included.

modules.title: Goal Setting and Fitness Plans
modules.objectives: Apply the SMART goal framework to fitness goals; build a structured personal training plan with measurable outcomes and timelines. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: CDC — Adding Physical Activity to Your Life
modules.videoNote: GIIS Physical Education — Module 7: Goal Setting and Fitness Plans — reviewed lesson video for this module.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Revise these three supplied vague goals for fictional students into SMART goals — “walk more,” “improve push-ups,” and “stretch regularly” — with supplied baselines of two 15-minute walks per week, six controlled wall push-ups, and one five-minute flexibility session per week — then build an eight-week calendar for one goal. Include a measurable baseline supplied in the scenario, weekly checkpoints, and one adjustment rule. Submit: the revised goals and calendar. Include: the required artifact, specific evidence from the fictional or provided data, and a brief explanation of the major choices. Evaluation: each goal is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound; checkpoints align with the goal; and the adjustment rule is realistic.

modules.title: Nutrition for Active People
modules.objectives: Identify macronutrients and their roles in exercise; explain pre- and post-workout nutrition strategies; apply hydration guidelines. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Physical Education — Module 8: Nutrition for Active People — reviewed lesson video for this module.
modules.practiceNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson, assigned course materials, and teacher-reviewed practice inside the GIIS course path; no external practice platform is required.
modules.assignment: Evaluate this supplied fictional schedule: 7:00 breakfast — oatmeal, banana, and water; 10:30 snack — crackers; 12:30 lunch — rice, beans, vegetables, and water; 4:00–5:00 soccer practice in warm weather with one 250 mL bottle of water; 5:30 snack — yogurt; 7:00 dinner — chicken, vegetables, and rice. Identify the roles of carbohydrate, protein, and fat; propose one pre-activity and one post-activity change; and create a practical hydration plan without supplements. Submit: an annotated schedule and a 150-word rationale. Include: the required artifact, specific evidence from the fictional or provided data, and a brief explanation of the major choices. Evaluation: nutrient roles are accurate; timing recommendations fit the scenario; hydration advice is reasonable; and claims avoid medical diagnosis. Do not submit a personal food diary.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the five health-related components of physical fitness?
quizQuestions.answer: Agility
quizQuestions.explanation: The five health-related components are cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, and body composition. Agility is a skill-related component.

quizQuestions.question: The ability of the heart and lungs to deliver oxygen to working muscles over a prolonged period is called:
options: Anaerobic power during one brief maximal effort
quizQuestions.answer: Cardiovascular endurance
quizQuestions.explanation: Cardiovascular endurance reflects how efficiently the cardiorespiratory system sustains aerobic activity.

quizQuestions.question: Which activity most directly demonstrates muscular endurance?
options: Holding one stretch for ten seconds
One controlled squat completed with near-maximal resistance
quizQuestions.answer: Twenty controlled body-weight squats
quizQuestions.explanation: Muscular endurance is the ability of a muscle group to repeat contractions over time; a controlled set of many repetitions demonstrates that capacity.

quizQuestions.question: Which fitness component describes a muscle producing its greatest force in one effort?
quizQuestions.answer: A complete response should answer this prompt directly: identify muscular strength and explain that it describes maximum force produced in one effort.
quizQuestions.explanation: Muscular strength describes the greatest force a muscle or muscle group can produce in a single effort.

quizQuestions.question: In the FITT principle, what does 'I' stand for?
quizQuestions.answer: Intensity
quizQuestions.explanation: FITT = Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type — the four variables used to design an exercise program.

quizQuestions.question: 'Frequency' in the FITT principle refers to:
options: What type of activity you do
How often you exercise per week
How many sets are completed during each exercise session
quizQuestions.answer: How often you exercise per week
quizQuestions.explanation: Frequency is how often activity occurs, commonly expressed as sessions per week; intensity, time, and type describe different parts of a FITT plan.

quizQuestions.question: Casey is a fictional 14-year-old beginner who can already walk comfortably for 30 minutes at a talk-test effort, has no pain, and has three activity days available. Which option is the best starting walking example for Casey's paper FITT plan?
options: 3 days/week at maximal intensity for 30 minutes
5 days/week at maximum intensity for 60 minutes
3 days/week at vigorous intensity for 30 minutes regardless of response
3 days/week at moderate intensity for 30 minutes
quizQuestions.answer: 3 days/week at moderate intensity for 30 minutes
quizQuestions.explanation: For Casey’s stated fictional walking profile, three moderate 30-minute sessions fit the demonstrated tolerance and schedule. It is a contextual example, not a universal beginner prescription. Hold or reduce workload for unusual difficulty or fatigue; stop a painful activity and tell a responsible adult or qualified professional.

quizQuestions.question: A student changes a plan from two workouts per week to three while keeping intensity, time, and type the same. Which FITT variable changed?
quizQuestions.answer: Frequency
quizQuestions.explanation: Frequency describes how often activity occurs. Adding a weekly session changes frequency while the other FITT variables remain constant.

quizQuestions.question: What does VO2 max estimate during intense aerobic exercise?
options: Maximum carbon dioxide consumption during intense exercise
Maximum oxygen consumption during intense exercise
quizQuestions.answer: Maximum oxygen consumption during intense exercise
quizQuestions.explanation: VO2 max represents the maximum rate at which the body can consume oxygen during maximal aerobic exercise.

quizQuestions.question: A lower resting heart rate generally indicates:
options: A short-term response caused only by dehydration or medication
quizQuestions.answer: Better cardiovascular fitness
quizQuestions.explanation: Well-trained hearts pump more blood per beat (greater stroke volume), beating fewer times per minute at rest.

quizQuestions.question: Which activity is primarily aerobic?
quizQuestions.answer: 30-minute jog
quizQuestions.explanation: Aerobic activity uses oxygen-dependent metabolism to release energy from carbohydrate and fat during sustained effort; oxygen itself is not an energy source.

quizQuestions.question: Which test most directly measures muscular endurance?
options: A vertical-jump test emphasizing explosive power
quizQuestions.answer: Timed push-up or sit-up test
quizQuestions.explanation: Muscular endurance tests measure how many repetitions a muscle can perform over time, not maximum force.

quizQuestions.question: The principle of specificity in strength training means:
options: Training adaptations are specific to the muscles and movements trained
All exercises are equally effective for all muscles
Strength gains transfer automatically to all sports
Specificity means choosing exercises by preference rather than by the target outcome
quizQuestions.answer: Training adaptations are specific to the muscles and movements trained
quizQuestions.explanation: Specificity means the body adapts to the muscles, movements, and energy demands actually trained, so a program should match its target outcome.

quizQuestions.question: Which muscle is primarily targeted by a push-up?
options: The anterior deltoid acting as the only prime mover
quizQuestions.answer: Pectoralis major
quizQuestions.explanation: Push-ups primarily work the pectoralis major (chest), assisted by the triceps and anterior deltoid.

quizQuestions.question: What change in muscle fibers is called hypertrophy?
options: Increase in muscle fiber size due to training
Improved coordination without a change in fiber size
quizQuestions.answer: Increase in muscle fiber size due to training
quizQuestions.explanation: Muscular hypertrophy is the enlargement of muscle fibers in response to resistance training.

quizQuestions.question: Static stretching is best performed:
options: After exercise when muscles are warm
First thing in the morning before any activity
Before explosive athletic activity as a warm-up
quizQuestions.answer: After exercise when muscles are warm
quizQuestions.explanation: Comfortable static stretching is commonly used after activity or when tissues are warm; timing and method should still match the person, activity, and range of motion.

quizQuestions.question: Dynamic stretching involves:
options: Slow passive holds maintained at the end of the available range
A partner pushing your limb past its range
Quick, uncontrolled bouncing at the end of the range
Controlled movements through a full range of motion
quizQuestions.answer: Controlled movements through a full range of motion
quizQuestions.explanation: Dynamic stretching uses controlled movements like leg swings and arm circles to prepare muscles for activity.

quizQuestions.question: Which warm-up choice best prepares the body for a planned activity?
options: General movements that remain unrelated to the planned activity
Skipping movement until the main activity begins
A long maximal static stretch while muscles are cold
Controlled movements that gradually resemble the activity
quizQuestions.answer: Controlled movements that gradually resemble the activity
quizQuestions.explanation: A dynamic warm-up uses controlled, progressively specific movement to prepare for the activity.

quizQuestions.question: What distinguishes PNF stretching from ordinary static stretching?
options: It alternates a muscle contraction with a stretch, often with trained guidance
It uses only fast bouncing movements
It holds a relaxed muscle at one position without a contraction phase
It is an aerobic endurance test
quizQuestions.answer: It alternates a muscle contraction with a stretch, often with trained guidance
quizQuestions.explanation: PNF methods combine contraction and relaxation with stretching; careful technique or qualified guidance helps control intensity.

quizQuestions.question: Which formula is used to calculate BMI?
options: Fat mass divided by lean mass
Waist circumference divided by total body weight
quizQuestions.answer: Weight divided by height squared
quizQuestions.explanation: BMI = weight (kg) / height (m)^2. It is a simple screening proxy for body weight status.

quizQuestions.question: Which method provides the most accurate body fat percentage measurement?
options: Single-site skinfold testing without a standardized protocol
quizQuestions.answer: Hydrostatic (underwater) weighing
quizQuestions.explanation: Hydrostatic weighing uses water displacement and Archimedes' principle to calculate body density and fat percentage accurately.

quizQuestions.question: Essential body fat is required for:
options: Storage of surplus energy without any hormonal or organ function
quizQuestions.answer: Normal physiological function
quizQuestions.explanation: Essential fat supports hormone production, organ protection, and other critical body functions.

quizQuestions.question: Why can BMI give an incomplete picture of an individual's body composition?
options: It does not distinguish fat mass from lean mass
It directly measures fat mass but omits cardiovascular fitness
quizQuestions.answer: It does not distinguish fat mass from lean mass
quizQuestions.explanation: BMI is based on weight relative to height and does not directly separate fat, muscle, bone, or other tissues.

quizQuestions.question: The 'M' in SMART goals stands for:
quizQuestions.answer: Measurable
quizQuestions.explanation: SMART = Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Measurable means clear criteria exist for tracking progress.

quizQuestions.question: Which is the best example of a SMART fitness goal?
options: I will run a 5K in under 30 minutes within 8 weeks by training 4 days per week
I want to be healthy someday
I will run a 5K under 30 minutes next month regardless of my baseline
quizQuestions.answer: I will run a 5K in under 30 minutes within 8 weeks by training 4 days per week
quizQuestions.explanation: The goal is specific, measurable, and time-bound. Whether it is achievable depends on the fictional student’s baseline and constraints, so a plan should check those before progression.

quizQuestions.question: Which revision makes the goal 'exercise more' measurable and time-bound?
options: Complete three walks each week without defining duration or an end date
Complete three 25-minute walks each week for the next six weeks
quizQuestions.answer: Complete three 25-minute walks each week for the next six weeks
quizQuestions.explanation: The revised goal specifies frequency, duration, and a six-week deadline, so progress can be measured.

quizQuestions.question: Carbohydrates are the preferred energy source for high-intensity exercise because they:
options: Are quickly broken down into glucose for immediate energy
Provide more energy per gram than fat
Must first be converted into amino acids before use
quizQuestions.answer: Are quickly broken down into glucose for immediate energy
quizQuestions.explanation: Carbohydrates are rapidly converted to glucose and glycogen, providing the primary fuel for high-intensity exercise.

quizQuestions.question: Which factor most directly changes how much fluid a person may need during activity?
options: Heat, activity frequency, and individual sweat rate
Heat, activity duration, and individual sweat rate
One fixed amount for every participant
quizQuestions.answer: Heat, activity duration, and individual sweat rate
quizQuestions.explanation: Fluid needs vary with environmental heat, how long activity lasts, and how much an individual sweats; a single fixed amount does not fit every situation.

quizQuestions.question: Protein is most important for athletes in order to:
options: Supply most immediate energy during short maximal competition
Support muscle repair and growth after exercise
Replace water and electrolytes lost through sweat
quizQuestions.answer: Support muscle repair and growth after exercise
quizQuestions.explanation: Protein provides amino acids essential for repairing exercise-damaged muscle tissue and building new fibers.

quizQuestions.question: Which choice best supports routine hydration during moderate activity?
options: Drink a fixed large amount regardless of heat or duration
Wait until thirst becomes intense before drinking, regardless of conditions
Begin hydrated and drink fluids at reasonable intervals based on conditions and duration
Use energy drinks for every short activity
quizQuestions.answer: Begin hydrated and drink fluids at reasonable intervals based on conditions and duration
quizQuestions.explanation: Hydration needs vary with heat, duration, and the person; beginning hydrated and drinking at reasonable intervals is safer than a rigid extreme.

questions.question: Which of the following is a health-related component of physical fitness?
options: Agility measured by rapid changes of direction during a drill
Coordination of balance and reaction skills
questions.answer: Cardiovascular endurance
questions.explanation: Health-related components: cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition.

questions.question: In the FITT principle, 'Time' refers to:
options: The hour of day you exercise
questions.answer: The duration of each session
questions.explanation: Time is the duration of each exercise session; frequency is how often sessions occur, intensity is effort, and type is the activity chosen.

questions.question: A student performs 3 sets of 15 push-ups. This primarily develops:
questions.answer: Muscular endurance
questions.explanation: A set of 15 repeated push-ups requires the involved muscles to sustain repeated contractions, which emphasizes muscular endurance.

questions.question: A common classroom estimate for maximum heart rate subtracts age from what number?
questions.explanation: The simple estimate often taught is 220 minus age, though individual values vary.

questions.question: Dynamic stretching differs from static stretching because dynamic stretching:
options: Uses controlled movement through a range of motion
questions.answer: Uses controlled movement through a range of motion
questions.explanation: Dynamic stretching involves purposeful movement, unlike static stretching which holds a fixed position.

questions.question: BMI is calculated from which relationship?
questions.answer: Weight relative to height squared
questions.explanation: BMI = weight (kg) / height (m)^2 — a screening proxy for body weight status.

questions.question: The overload principle states that to improve fitness you must:
options: Train at maximum intensity from day one
Keep all workouts the same intensity
Stress the body beyond its current level to produce adaptation
questions.answer: Stress the body beyond its current level to produce adaptation
questions.explanation: Progressive overload — gradually increasing demand — is the foundation of fitness improvement.

questions.question: During high-intensity exercise, the body's preferred fuel source is usually what?
questions.answer: Carbohydrate
questions.explanation: Carbohydrate is generally easier to use quickly during high-intensity effort.

questions.question: Which change would shift a resistance exercise toward muscular strength rather than muscular endurance?
options: Use very light resistance for many more repetitions
Replace the exercise with static stretching
Use greater resistance for fewer controlled repetitions
questions.answer: Use greater resistance for fewer controlled repetitions
questions.explanation: Strength training generally emphasizes greater resistance and fewer controlled repetitions, while endurance training uses lower resistance for more repetitions.

questions.question: A beginner completes a comfortable walking plan for two weeks. Which progression best follows the FITT principle?
options: Increase one variable gradually, such as adding five minutes per session
Increase every FITT variable at once after one comfortable week
Reduce training time whenever the current plan feels comfortable
questions.answer: Increase one variable gradually, such as adding five minutes per session
questions.explanation: Changing one FITT variable gradually lets the body adapt and makes it easier to monitor the response.

questions.question: The sit-and-reach assessment tests:
questions.answer: Flexibility
questions.explanation: The sit-and-reach test measures flexibility, primarily of the hamstrings and lower back.

questions.question: Why do SMART goals help athletes plan improvement?
options: They make goals vague on purpose
They provide clear, measurable direction and timelines
They remove the need for practice
questions.answer: They provide clear, measurable direction and timelines
questions.explanation: SMART goals state a specific outcome, a way to measure it, and a deadline, which makes progress visible and supports planned adjustments.

questions.question: What physiological capacity does VO2 max estimate?
options: Maximum oxygen uptake during intense aerobic exercise
Maximum oxygen uptake during intense anaerobic exercise
questions.answer: Maximum oxygen uptake during intense aerobic exercise
questions.explanation: VO2 max estimates the greatest rate at which the body can use oxygen during intense aerobic effort, a measure of aerobic capacity.

questions.question: Muscular hypertrophy refers to:
options: Increased size of muscle fibers due to training
Decreased size of muscle fibers due to training
questions.answer: Increased size of muscle fibers due to training
questions.explanation: Hypertrophy is the enlargement of existing muscle fibers in response to resistance training.

questions.question: Which activity best develops cardiovascular endurance?
questions.answer: 45-minute cycling session
questions.explanation: Sustained aerobic activities like 45-minute cycling best develop cardiovascular endurance.

questions.question: What does the principle of specificity mean in fitness training?
options: Training adaptations are specific to the activity and demands practiced
All exercises improve all components equally
Cardiorespiratory training automatically produces maximal strength gains
questions.answer: Training adaptations are specific to the activity and demands practiced
questions.explanation: Specificity means the body adapts to the particular type of training it receives.

questions.question: A student changes from walking to cycling while keeping frequency, intensity, and time the same. Which FITT variable changed?
questions.answer: Type
questions.explanation: Type identifies the kind of activity. Changing from walking to cycling changes type while the schedule, effort, and duration stay constant.

questions.question: Essential body fat is necessary for:
options: Normal energy storage without any role in hormone production or organ protection
Normal physiological functions including hormone production and organ protection
questions.answer: Normal physiological functions including hormone production and organ protection
questions.explanation: Essential fat supports critical body functions and cannot be eliminated without serious health consequences.

questions.question: During regular aerobic training, which adaptation can help the heart supply blood more efficiently?
questions.answer: Greater stroke volume
questions.explanation: A trained heart can pump more blood per beat, helping deliver oxygen during sustained activity.

questions.question: During sustained aerobic activity, cardiovascular endurance helps the body by:
options: Increasing joint range of motion directly
Delivering oxygen to working muscles over time
Delivering carbon dioxide to working muscles over time
Producing maximal force in one contraction
questions.answer: Delivering oxygen to working muscles over time
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular endurance reflects how effectively the heart, lungs, and blood vessels supply oxygen during sustained activity.

questions.question: Which resistance-training plan best applies gradual overload?
options: Decrease resistance or repetitions in small steps after the current workload is performed with control
Begin every session with a maximal attempt
Increase resistance or repetitions in small steps after the current workload is performed with control
Change all variables sharply at once
questions.answer: Increase resistance or repetitions in small steps after the current workload is performed with control
questions.explanation: Gradual overload increases demand enough to promote adaptation while preserving control and allowing the response to be monitored.

questions.question: Glycogen stores are primarily depleted during:
options: Prolonged low-intensity activity with frequent rest breaks
questions.answer: Prolonged moderate-to-high intensity exercise
questions.explanation: Glycogen is the primary fuel for moderate-to-high intensity exercise and becomes significantly depleted during prolonged sessions.

questions.question: Which preparation is appropriate before explosive athletic activity?
options: A dynamic warm-up including movement preparation
A long static hold followed immediately by a maximal explosive effort
questions.answer: A dynamic warm-up including movement preparation
questions.explanation: Dynamic warm-ups increase heart rate, blood flow, and muscle temperature while activating neuromuscular patterns needed for sport.

questions.question: Which sequence best uses dynamic and static stretching?
options: Long maximal static holds before any warm-up
No warm-up before activity, followed by stretching only if discomfort appears
Controlled dynamic movements before activity and comfortable static stretches after activity or when warm
Fast bouncing before and after every activity
questions.answer: Controlled dynamic movements before activity and comfortable static stretches after activity or when warm
questions.explanation: Dynamic movement can prepare for activity, while comfortable static stretching is commonly used after activity or when tissues are warm.

questions.question: Which is the best SMART fitness goal?
options: Complete as many push-ups as possible next month without a baseline or schedule
Complete 10 more push-ups than my current max within 4 weeks, training 3 days/week
questions.answer: Complete 10 more push-ups than my current max within 4 weeks, training 3 days/week
questions.explanation: This goal names the exercise, measurable improvement, four-week deadline, and weekly training frequency, so progress can be checked.

questions.question: How should BMI be interpreted for adolescents?
options: With adult cutoffs only, regardless of age
As an age-and-sex-specific diagnostic percentile, not a direct body-fat diagnosis
As an exact measure of muscle mass
As an age-and-sex-specific screening percentile, not a direct body-fat diagnosis
questions.answer: As an age-and-sex-specific screening percentile, not a direct body-fat diagnosis
questions.explanation: Because adolescents are still growing, BMI is interpreted by age-and-sex percentiles and used as a screening measure rather than a diagnosis.

questions.question: Dehydration during exercise causes:
options: Decreased performance, decreased heat-illness risk, and impaired cognition
Decreased performance, increased heat-illness risk, and impaired cognition
questions.answer: Decreased performance, increased heat-illness risk, and impaired cognition
questions.explanation: Even mild dehydration (2% body weight loss) reduces aerobic performance and increases heat illness risk.

questions.question: Which statement accurately distinguishes lean mass from fat mass?
options: Lean mass is only muscle and excludes bone
Fat mass includes only essential fat and excludes stored fat
Lean mass includes muscle, bone, organs, and body water; fat mass is stored and essential fat
questions.answer: Lean mass includes muscle, bone, organs, and body water; fat mass is stored and essential fat
questions.explanation: Body composition separates fat mass from fat-free or lean tissues; essential fat also supports normal physiological function.

questions.question: PNF stretching achieves greater range of motion by:
options: Using alternating muscle contraction and relaxation
Holding a relaxed muscle at a fixed end-range position without contraction
questions.answer: Using alternating muscle contraction and relaxation
questions.explanation: PNF exploits the neurological stretch reflex — alternating contraction and relaxation allows muscles to lengthen further.

questions.question: A SMART plan misses two weekly checkpoints. What is the best evidence-based adjustment?
options: Increase every weekly workload immediately before reviewing why checkpoints were missed
Declare the goal impossible without checking evidence
Erase the checkpoints and stop measuring
Review the record, identify the barrier, and revise one realistic plan variable
questions.answer: Review the record, identify the barrier, and revise one realistic plan variable
questions.explanation: SMART plans use measurable checkpoints as feedback; a focused, realistic adjustment responds to evidence without abandoning the goal.

questions.question: Why is a gradual cool-down useful after sustained exercise?
options: An abrupt stop is safer because cardiovascular demand falls immediately
Allows activity intensity and circulation demands to decrease progressively
questions.answer: Allows activity intensity and circulation demands to decrease progressively
questions.explanation: A gradual cool-down lets cardiovascular demand fall progressively and can reduce abrupt light-headedness; it is not required to “flush” lactic acid.

questions.question: Which assessment best measures muscular strength?
options: A high-repetition push-up test continued until technique begins to fail
questions.answer: One-repetition maximum (1RM) test
questions.explanation: A 1RM test estimates maximal force for a specific lift; the PACER measures aerobic endurance.

questions.question: Which macronutrient supplies amino acids used to repair and build body tissues?
questions.answer: Protein
questions.explanation: Protein is digested into amino acids that the body uses to maintain and repair tissues; carbohydrate and fat serve different major roles.

questions.question: Which is an example of an aerobic activity?
options: A sequence of ten maximal 10-second sprints separated by complete rest
questions.answer: 30-minute dance class
questions.explanation: Aerobic activities are sustained, moderate-intensity exercises relying on oxygen. A 30-minute dance class qualifies.

questions.question: Which checkpoint best evaluates progress toward the SMART goal 'complete three 25-minute walks weekly for six weeks'?
options: Record completed sessions and minutes at the end of each week
Judge progress only by how motivated the person feels
Wait until the year ends before checking
Compare the plan only with another person's weekly total
questions.answer: Record completed sessions and minutes at the end of each week
questions.explanation: Weekly session and duration records directly measure the stated behavior and allow timely adjustments.
